item.title: Your Adult Child Doesn't Want Your Silence
item.description:
Parenting

Your Adult Child Doesn't Want Your Silence

Honesty isn't a fight—it's the relationship you've been skipping.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Honest communication and confrontation are not the same thing—one attacks, the other reveals.
  • Your needs don't disappear just because you're the parent. They've just gone unspoken.
  • A parent who never pushes back isn't modeling peace. They're modeling disappearance.

One of my favorite songs, by the Foo Fighters, begins with the line, "I've got another confession to make." Well, to all you parents reading this, I have a confession: years ago, I used to passively watch moms and dads sit on their hands in my office or in virtual sessions, sharing stories of mistaking silence for maturity. They'd tell me, "I don't want to rock the boat," as if honesty and confrontation were the same thing.

By the way, they are not the same thing. The moment a parent imagines speaking their truth, their brain jumps to a Thanksgiving screaming match. At least those are the types of inner fears that parents reveal to me. So they say nothing instead, year after year, and call it keeping the peace—when really it's keeping themselves out of the relationship entirely.

Try This Instead of Silence

I want to be clear about what I'm actually suggesting, because it isn't what most parents fear. There's a way to be honest that is neither confrontational nor silent. It comes down to one shift: talk about your own experience, not about the other person's behavior.

Take Jenny, the mother I worked with who hadn't heard from her son in three weeks. Her old instinct was to say "You never call me anymore," which, after she sounded it out, she realized sounded more like a verdict than a conversation. Once we talked this through, she tried: "When we go a few weeks without talking, I find myself wondering if something's wrong, and I get worried." She expressed the same feeling but with zero ammunition. Her son surprisingly didn't get defensive—he got honest back.

Or the father who shared with me that he realized pride doesn't count if you never say it out loud. "I'm proud of how far you've come, and I want to say that directly, because I don't think I've said it enough." This isn't confrontation, it's just true. Yet, for a lot of parents, said out loud, it's basically a foreign language. I can tell you that many adult children confide in me that hearing "I'm proud of you for..." from their parents still warms their hearts.

The Avoidance-Rescuing-Resentment Trap

When there are kinds of contrived politeness, the deeper issue is that nobody wants to face the issues directly. That's a setup I hear about a lot from parents who are in emotoinal pain. Because somewhere along the way, a lot of these parents absorbed an idea, never spoken, rarely examined, that in this particular relationship, their needs simply don't count. That they're allowed to be worried, hurt, or disconnected... just not out loud.

I wrote an entire book about where that thinking leads, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me! , because I kept seeing the same pattern: parents who stayed quiet for so long that quiet turned into rescuing, and rescuing turned into resentment nobody would name. Silence doesn't just cost you your voice. It can cost you the very relationship you were trying to protect.

article continues after advertisement

Show Up as a Whole Person

Reclaiming your voice means letting what you actually experience back into the relationship. I'm talking about being willing to say a comment stung, that you've felt distant, that you miss your kid. Obviously, you're not going to say these things in a way to pick a fight, but rather to say, "Hey, I want us to engage in a calm, constructive conversation that benefits both of us." This allows you to show up as a whole person again, opinions and limits included, instead of the quiet, accommodating background character you've been auditioning for.

Here's the part that surprises parents most: that presence (even when it feels a little shaky) is a gift, not a burden. An adult child who has only ever known a parent who never pushes back, never names a need, never asserts a limit, hasn't been shown extra love. They've been shown absence dressed up as agreeableness and never seen what a healthy relationship between two full people actually looks like.

The Takeaway

You don't owe anyone your disappearance. Speak up and do it quietly, yet honestly, and, most importantly, like you matter, because you do.

item.title: On the Origin of the Healthy Mind
item.description:
Intelligence

On the Origin of the Healthy Mind

Why a new perspective on mental health is a cultural imperative

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • The mind is not separate from nature. It is nature evolved.
  • When a society neglects the natural evolution of our mind, it endangers mental well-being.
  • When symbolic intelligence is divorced from embodiment, nature, and community, it can become dangerous.
  • Mental health requires attunement with the living intelligence that shapes us.
A healthy mind is an intelligent phenomenon that is alive.
Source: Leo Rivas/Unsplash

A Blind Spot With Real‑World Consequences

Richard Davidson, the founder and director of the Center for Healthy Minds at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, warns us (Davidson & Dahl, 2026, p 5):

“The human species is experiencing a massive mental health crisis.”

Over 150 years have passed since the publication of On the Origin of Species (Darwin, 1859), and biological evolution has since become a cornerstone of modern science. We now accept that species adapt, transform, and sometimes become extinct. We use evolutionary principles to study disease, ecology, and behavior.

However, when it comes to the human mind, acceptance suddenly wavers. We hesitate to view mental life—perception, consciousness, and identity—as part of the same evolutionary continuum. This hesitation is not just intellectual curiosity. It is a public health issue of the highest order.

If the mind is an evolutionary phenomenon, then its health depends on the living processes that shape it. When a society neglects these processes, it endangers mental well-being. This is the forgotten evolution, and its consequences are visible everywhere (De Vleeschauwer, 2026).

How the Mind Became “Non‑Natural”

For centuries, Western thought has treated the human mind as separate from nature. Descartes separated thinking from matter (Descartes, 1641). Kant placed rationality in a transcendental realm (Kant, 1781). Early psychology adopted this dualistic perspective, focusing on functions, symbols, and cognition rather than biological evolution.

This created a powerful cultural assumption. Intelligence is cultural, not biological. Intelligence is symbolic, not evolutionary. Intelligence is human, not natural. However, modern science increasingly contradicts this view.

Darwin Was Visible—The Mind Is Not

Darwin’s theory convinced the world because its premises were observable: fossils, anatomical variation, ecological pressures, and natural selection. By contrast, the mind leaves no fossils. It cannot be excavated or weighed. It only emerges in interaction between organism and environment, body and brain, and person and culture. This invisibility has delayed our understanding of mental evolution. However, it has not stopped progress.

article continues after advertisement

The New Science: The Mind Is Evolutionary

A new consensus is emerging across biology, neuroscience, and cognitive science: Intelligence is not a human exception, but rather a life function. Cells sense and respond to information (Miller, 2020; Levin, 2021). Plants demonstrate perception, memory, and problem-solving abilities (Mancuso & Viola, 2015; Calvo & Friston, 2017). The brain is a predictive organ that continuously adjusts to its environment (Friston, 2010). Evolution is driven by cooperation and information exchange (Margulis, 1998).

In this light, the human mind becomes easier to understand. It is a late evolutionary refinement of the same living intelligence that shaped all organisms. The mind is not separate from nature. It is nature evolved.

The Human Mind as an Evolutionary Organ

Viewing the mind through an evolutionary lens provides four key insights.

1. Perception is biological attunement. Our senses act as active filters, shaped by millions of years of adaptation (LeDoux, 2019, 2023).

2. Consciousness is relational. It emerges from the interplay between the body, brain, environment, and culture (Damasio, 2026).

3. Identity is dynamic. The self is an evolving pattern of interactions (Thompson, 2007).

4. Thinking is a recent development.

Symbolic reasoning is an extension of older forms of sensing and resonating (Reber, 2019). In other words: The mind is not an exception to evolution; rather, it is one of evolution’s most complex outcomes.

The Crucial Insight: Mental Health Has an Evolutionary Origin

This is where the societal relevance becomes clear. If the mind is evolutionary, then mental health depends on conditions that foster evolutionary intelligence, such as sensory richness, ecological connection, relational warmth, embodied presence, and a sense of meaning rooted in lived experience.

These are not luxuries. They are biological necessities. Modern society is eroding them. We live indoors, on screens, and in abstraction. We move less, sense less, and relate less. We overload our cognition and starve our perception. This is not a neutral shift. It is an evolutionary mismatch—a gap between what our minds evolved to need and what our culture provides.

The result is evident in the rising rates of anxiety, depression, burnout, loneliness, fragmented attention, and identity instability. These are not just psychological disorders. Rather, they are symptoms of disconnection from the processes that sustain mental health. This is why the title matters. On the Origin of the Healthy Mind is not a metaphor. It is a literal description of where mental health comes from—and what we are losing.

article continues after advertisement

The Human Paradox: Highest Intelligence, Highest Vulnerability

Symbolic intelligence endows humans with extraordinary abilities, such as imagination, planning, creativity, and cooperation. However, it also enables us to detach from the ecological and relational realities that shaped us. When abstraction is divorced from embodiment, nature, and community, it becomes dangerous. This evolutionary tension lies at the heart of modern mental health.

Restoring Attunement: A Public Health Priority

If the mind is an evolutionary organ, then mental health requires attunement—reconnection with the living systems that shaped us.

1. Ecological attunement: nature contact, rhythm, sensory grounding, and movement.

2. Relational attunement: healthy attachment, empathy, co-regulation, and shared meaning.

3. Cognitive attunement: model awareness, emotional sensitivity, and metacognition.

These are not therapeutic techniques. They are evolutionary conditions. Neglecting them is not just unhealthy—it is unsustainable.

Conclusion: The Forgotten Evolution and the Future of Mental Health

The evolution of the human mind is not a speculative idea. Rather, it is a necessary extension of Darwin’s insight. As living organisms, we developed a new form of attunement: symbolic intelligence. Because of this, we stand at a cultural and ecological crossroads.

Understanding the mind in evolutionary terms does not diminish humanity. Rather, it situates us within the living world and reminds us that mental health is biological and ecological as well as psychological.

The missing evolution is not biological. It is psychological. Recognizing this may be one of the most important steps we can take toward a healthier, more connected future.

article continues after advertisement

D. H. Lawrence reminds us in poetic fashion of the importance of the living intelligence of a healthy mind:

“Whatever the unborn and the dead may know, they cannot know the beauty, the marvel of being alive in the flesh.”

Can we ever overcome the massive mental health crisis we are facing if we don’t see ourselves as part of the evolution of living intelligence?
